transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

My primary care doctor referred me to you because I’ve been struggling so much since my cousin passed away. I go out of my way to avoid anything that reminds me of what happened to him, even if it means cutting out parts of my life. It has just become too hard to manage on my own.
Are you having intrusive thoughts or memories about your cousin’s death that cause significant distress, or do the avoidant behaviors mainly stem from a general sense of sadness or loss?

It's definitely more than just sadness. Out of nowhere, I’ll suddenly see my cousin's body in the coffin or hear my aunt describing the shooting, and my chest tightens and I just freeze. I avoid buses, Spanish news, and community events because I’m terrified that encountering anything related to it will make me completely fall apart.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["F43.1", "F32.0", "F42.2"], but based on this conversation, F32.0 (depressive episode, mild) and F42.2 (mixed obsessive-compulsive disorder) are less likely. The patient describes trauma-specific intrusive memories (e.g., seeing the cousin's body, hearing descriptions of the shooting), marked avoidance of trauma-related stimuli (buses, Spanish news, community events), and intense psychological distress to cues—core features of post-traumatic stress disorder. There is no indication of persistent low mood, anhedonia, or obsessive rituals that would support depression or OCD. Therefore, F43.1 (post-traumatic stress disorder) remains the most consistent diagnosis.
